segments.text: Before the new run: what did veḷḷostānu mean?
కృతజ్ఞత (kṛtajñata) — "gratitude".
kṛta, "done", plus jña, "knowing": knowing what was done for you. That is the whole of gratitude in two Sanskrit syllables, and Telugu took it entire.

Set it beside ధన్యవాదములు, the thank-you from the first pages of this book, which is "utterances of 'worthy'". One word thanks by calling the giver worthy. The other thanks by admitting the debt is remembered. They are not the same gesture, and Telugu keeps both.
A second word for thanks, with a different picture inside it.

segments.instruction: kṛtajñata
it once more, slowly
kṛtajñata, then dhanyavādamulu, and say which one remembers a debt
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kṛtajñata*, then *dhanyavādamulu*, and say which one remembers a debt]

segments.text: What does కృతజ్ఞత (kṛtajñata) mean? ("gratitude".) Say it once more.

lessons.title: ఞ (ña) — one character, met inside a word you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ఞ — recognised inside a word you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ఞ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ృ — what does it do? And one from further back: భ?
One character this time — and you have been saying it since the page before this one, without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ఞ — ña.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ñ, it is ña.

It is a nasal, made where య is made — the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth, the sound in the middle of Spanish señor. In modern Telugu you will almost never meet it standing on its own. Where it lives is inside one stacked block, and you met that block a moment ago:
కృతజ్ఞత kṛtajñata — gratitude.

The block is జ్ఞ: జ with ఞ stacked under it, joined by the virama. Telugu does not say that block the way its two letters would suggest. Spelled jña, it comes out of the mouth closer to gnya — so kṛtajñata is heard as kṛtagnyata. Both facts are true at once, and this is one of the places where Telugu's spelling remembers Sanskrit while Telugu's mouth has moved on.

blocks.title: Writing: ఞ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ఞ (ña) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at కృతజ్ఞత (kṛtajñata), and find the block that has ఞ under it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at కృతజ్ఞత, and find the block that has ఞ under it]

segments.text: కృతజ్ఞత (kṛtajñata), ధన్యవాదములు.

segments.instruction: ఞ three times, saying ña as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ఞ three times, saying *ña* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: kṛtajñata the way it is said — kṛtagnyata
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *kṛtajñata* the way it is said — *kṛtagnyata*]

segments.text: Which character is this — ఞ (ña)? Which letter does it usually sit under, and what does that pair sound like? (Under జ, in the block జ్ఞ, said gnya.)
One more, from much earlier: ◌ై — what does it do?

lessons.title: మేలు (mēlu) — a good turn, a benefit

segments.text: Before the new one: what did kṛtajñata mean?
మేలు (mēlu) — "a good turn, a benefit".
Inherited, and short. మేల్ meant "above"; the good is what is above. From it Telugu draws మేలు (mēlu), a benefit or a good turn done to someone, and also the plain comparative sense of "better".
So idi mēlu says "this one is higher" and lets the height do the judging --- which is what English does too, in superior, without anyone noticing any more.
Two.

segments.instruction: mēlu

mēlu, then manci, and say which one is a thing done and which is a quality
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *mēlu*, then *manci*, and say which one is a thing done and which is a quality]

segments.text: What does మేలు (mēlu) mean? ("a good turn, a benefit".) Say it once more.
Before the new one: what did mēlu mean?
గౌరవం (gauravaṁ) — "respect".
gaurava is the abstract noun of guru --- the very word met one chapter ago as the teacher. Respect is weightiness: to hold someone in గౌరవం (gauravaṁ) is to grant that what they say has mass.

Telugu marks the same idea in its grammar as well as its vocabulary. మీరు rather than నువ్వు, and the -అండి hung on the end of a verb, are గౌరవం (gauravaṁ) turned into endings. A language can be polite in its words or in its shapes, and this one does both.
Three, and one of them is a word you already knew wearing a different suit.

segments.instruction: gauravaṁ
it once more, slowly
gauravaṁ, then guruvu, and name the syllable they share
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *gauravaṁ*, then *guruvu*, and name the syllable they share]

segments.text: What does గౌరవం (gauravaṁ) mean? ("respect".) Say it once more.

lessons.title: ◌ౌ (au) — one character, met inside a word you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ౌ — recognised inside a word you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌ౌ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ఞ (ña) — what does it do? And one from further back: ఋ?
One character this time — and you have been saying it since the page before this one, without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with au. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
Au is one vowel that moves while you hold it: it starts where a starts and slides toward u, the way the middle of English now does. Say it as one sound, not as two.
You already say this one:
గౌరవం gauravaṁ — respect.

Take it apart: గ, the letter you traced long before this, carrying ◌ౌ. Not ga any more — gau. Then ర, వ, and the anusvāra ం that has been closing words since namaskāram. Every piece of gauravaṁ now has a name, and this mark was the last one missing.
Put your pen on ◌ౌ (au) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these two, and say which one carries ◌ౌ (au)
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these two, and say which one carries ◌ౌ]

segments.text: గౌరవం (gauravaṁ), గురువు.

segments.instruction: ga, then gau, and hear the vowel move
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ga*, then *gau*, and hear the vowel move]

segments.instruction: ◌ౌ three times, saying au as you finish each one

segments.text: Which character is this — ◌ౌ? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to, and what does it take off? (Puts au on; takes the built-in a off.) Name the word you already say that contains it.
One more, from much earlier: ఖ — what does it do?
Before the new one: what did gauravaṁ mean?
ఆశీర్వాదం (āśīrvādaṁ) — "a blessing".
āśīs, a wish or a prayer, plus vāda, an utterance: a blessing is a wish said out loud.

The ceremony behind it is still in daily use. You bend and touch an elder's feet, and what comes back is ఆశీర్వాదం (āśīrvādaṁ) --- a hand on the head --- at a birthday, before an examination, at a wedding, and at every departure.
Notice vāda sitting there. It is the same piece inside ధన్యవాదములు, "utterances of 'worthy'". Twice now this language has counted a thing said as a thing given.
Four courtesy words, and two of them are utterances by name.

segments.instruction: āśīrvādaṁ
it once more, slowly
āśīrvādaṁ, then dhanyavādamulu, and name the piece they share
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *āśīrvādaṁ*, then *dhanyavādamulu*, and name the piece they share]

segments.text: What does ఆశీర్వాదం (āśīrvādaṁ) mean? ("a blessing".) Say it once more.
Before the new one: what did āśīrvādaṁ mean?
దండం (daṇḍaṁ) — "a salutation, "my respects"".
దండం (daṇḍaṁ) is what you say with the palms together --- my respects --- offered to an elder, a temple, a photograph on the wall. Children are taught to say it long before anyone explains it.

Sanskrit daṇḍa is a staff, a stick. The full form of the gesture, daṇḍa-praṇāma, is the prostration where the body lies down straight as a staff. Telugu kept the word and let the body straighten most of the way up.
Hold on to దండ; it comes back in the next chapter carrying flowers.
Five courtesy words: కృతజ్ఞత (kṛtajñata), మేలు (mēlu), గౌరవం (gauravaṁ), ఆశీర్వాదం (āśīrvādaṁ), దండం (daṇḍaṁ). Thanks, a good turn, respect, a blessing, and the greeting you make with your hands.
